paragraphs: The second breakfast was better.

Darius replaced the porridge with toasted bread, beans warmed in a pan, and a bowl of chopped apples that he had coaxed from a driver the previous week. The apples had a few soft spots, but everybody took some. In their part of the country, fresh fruit wasn't something you left behind because it looked imperfect.
Nico arrived carrying two plates and claimed the largest pieces of toast by moving them onto his own before setting anything down.
Darius caught him in the act.
“Those are for everyone,” Darius said.
“I'm part of everyone.”
“You're the part that hasn't helped.”
“I gave moral support during the porridge crisis.”
“You laughed.”
“With feeling.”
Andrew slid one of Nico's plates back toward the middle. “We appreciate your service.”
Nico made a face, but he let the plate go.

Mara spread her map across the table after the dishes had been cleared. Andrew moved his coffee away from the paper. Rain pressed softly against the high windows, and the radio on the shelf murmured through the morning bulletin. There were reports of another road closure farther east and the familiar request for civilians to conserve fuel. Nobody turned the volume up.
A thick blue pencil line crossed the map, following the patrol route from their depot to a relay station near the outer defensive works.

“The approach here has gone under,” Mara said. Her finger rested on the eastern crossing. “The water's already against the road markers. If the river keeps rising, we won't get a recovery vehicle through.”
“Can an XR-17 cross it?” Andrew asked.
“Probably. But if one of us has to tow another one home, we'd be stuck.”

Andrew pictured the route from memory. An open stretch of road, a narrow bridge, and a bend that concealed the next field until a pilot was almost on top of it. He had liked the direct approach because it kept the unit in sight of the observation post for most of the journey.
“Service road?” he asked.
Mara nodded and traced a line to the south. “Longer. Wider turn, though. We can pass the maintenance buildings and come in behind the station.”
“What's the downside?”
“Two extra kilometers, poor visibility at the drainage culvert, and Nico will complain about it.”
“I'm standing right here,” Nico said.
“Then I can strike the last one.”
Andrew studied the alternative route. Three weeks ago he might have made the decision before Mara had finished her explanation. Now he made himself ask the next question.
“Where would you bring a disabled machine around?”

Mara pointed out a hard-surfaced lot just beyond the culvert. She had already drawn the towing path in pencil. It would take longer, but none of their machines would have to back into the ditch to turn.
“That's the route,” Andrew said. “Mark the recovery point. We'll tell the others during checks.”
Mara looked pleasantly surprised for an instant, then disguised it by rolling up the map.
“You're getting easier to work with.”
“That's the nicest thing you've ever said to me.”
“Don't get used to it.”

Andrew watched her leave, the map tucked neatly under her arm. The morning schedule still had to be completed, the machines had to be inspected, and they had an afternoon test to run. Yet for the first time that day he felt a little less late.
At nine, the hangar doors were open enough to admit a gray stripe of daylight.

Inside, their XR-17s filled the maintenance bays like a line of resting animals. Each stood low on six articulated legs. Heavy armor covered the compact hulls, but joints and hydraulic lines remained visible wherever the plating needed to move. Their main cannons sat on rotating turrets above the angular cockpits, with matched upright missile pods on either side. Beneath each cockpit's armored brow, a smaller rotary cannon faced forward. The circular reactors projected from the rear of the machines, surrounded by cooling housings and service rails.

They were built to fight, not to be elegant. Up close, Andrew could see every repair their crews had made: replacement bolts in mismatched finishes, paint of slightly different shades, welds that no factory inspector would have accepted. Germany had produced the machines quickly enough to hold its ground when other defenses failed. Keeping these particular eight running was now up to the people living beside them.
Juno Kade was halfway underneath the left front leg of his machine.

Andrew recognized him by his bright golden-blond hair, which stuck out in directions no helmet could have caused. His orange goggles had been pushed up onto his forehead, and his headphones hung from the raised yellow collar of his dark jacket. A smear of black grease traveled from his wrist almost to his elbow.
“Morning,” Andrew called.
“Technically,” Juno replied from beneath the machine.
“What are we technically doing?”
“Removing a bearing.”
“Are we succeeding?”
“One of us is.”
Nico, kneeling beside a tray of parts, lifted a gloved hand. “That's me.”
Juno slid out on a low trolley and sat up. His bright blue eyes went from Andrew to the parts tray and back again.
“The left-front bearing's binding under load,” he said. “I felt it on the return yesterday. There's a replacement in stores, but the retaining collar doesn't want to come off.”

Andrew crouched to inspect the raised leg. A steel stand held its weight while the pistons were locked out. The bearing housing was partly disassembled, and the assembly had been marked so its alignment could be restored.
“You logged it?” Andrew asked.
“Yesterday.”
“And the new bearing?”
“Still wrapped. I was going to finish this before lunch, run a walking cycle, then check it again once everything cools.”
Andrew nodded. “Good. If it catches again, we ground the machine.”
Juno's mouth twisted. “You know what they sent us last time we asked for bearings?”
“A very polite refusal.”
“A request to explain why we couldn't reuse the old ones.”
Nico looked up. “We could send them the old one with a note saying it tried to eat the rest of the leg.”
“Don't,” Andrew said.
Juno considered it. “What if the note is formal?”
“Especially don't.”

On the next bay, a soft click sounded from a portable diagnostic screen. Sera Bell sat cross-legged on a crate with the cable looped around one knee. Her long curls were pinned into a loose bun, and she wore a large sweater over her work clothes. She was studying the recorded loads from Juno's last run.
“It's not just the bearing,” she said without looking up.
Juno turned. “You told me the bearing.”
“I told you the bearing was bad. There's also a loose vibration pickup on the left side. Your graph keeps saying the whole leg has fallen off, which would be more convincing if it actually had.”
Andrew glanced at the machine. “It hasn't, has it?”
Sera finally looked up.
“Not yet,” she said.
Juno groaned. “I knew you were going to say that.”

Sera unplugged the reader and held out the screen. She had highlighted the real bearing temperature and the false sensor spikes in different colors. Andrew saw the distinction immediately once she showed it to him.
“I can replace the pickup while he works on the collar,” Sera said.
“Do it,” Andrew answered. “And put both results on the inspection sheet. I want Mara to see them before we clear tomorrow's route.”
“You keep asking us to write down everything we fix,” Juno said.
“That's because you keep fixing things I didn't know were broken.”
“That's just good initiative.”
“It's excellent initiative,” Andrew said. “When it comes with paperwork.”
Juno sighed dramatically and rolled back under the leg.

Andrew stayed long enough to help Nico move the parts tray out of a puddle left by the leaking roof. He could have taken over. He knew how to hold the collar steady and how to thread the extractor, and the small voice that told him he'd sleep better if he did everything himself was already making its case.
Instead he left Juno to the work Juno knew best.
At the doors, he found Mara waiting with the revised map.
“Are we good?” she asked.
“Juno will tell us after the cold test. Sera's checking the sensor too.”
Mara studied his face. “And you didn't order them to let you help?”
“I moved a tray.”
“Miracles do happen.”
Andrew took the map from her. “Write that in the morning report.”
